posts.title: Best Climbing Shoes for Beginners: 7 Picks and How to Size Them
posts.excerpt: Seven flat, comfortable first pairs, the sizing advice that ruins most beginners, closure types, foot shape, and when upgrading is actually justified.
posts.content:
Almost everyone buys the wrong first pair. The best climbing shoes for beginners are not the ones the strong climber at your gym is wearing, and they are not the aggressively downturned models that dominate the "best of" lists — those are built for steep overhangs and hard edging, and on a beginner's foot they mostly just hurt.

This guide covers what actually matters in a first pair, seven shoes genuinely suited to it, the sizing advice that ruins more beginners' experience than anything else, and when it is worth upgrading. If you want the broader performance picture once you have a season behind you, our roundup of the best climbing shoes for rock climbers covers the more aggressive end.

What Makes a Good First Pair

Climbing shoes fall into three broad profiles, and the difference is not cosmetic.

Neutral shoes sit flat, like a normal shoe. Your foot stays in a natural position, which means you can wear them for an hour or more at a time. They have a stiffer sole that supports the foot on small edges without your toes doing the work. This is what a beginner wants.

Moderate shoes have a slight downward camber. A good second pair, and a reasonable first pair for someone who is already active and expects to climb several times a week.

Aggressive shoes are strongly downturned, with the toes forced into a curled, pointed shape to concentrate power on tiny holds. They are excellent on steep terrain and genuinely painful to stand around in. Beginners who buy these usually stop climbing sooner, because sessions become something to endure.

The reasoning is simple. In your first year, the limiting factor is technique, not shoe performance. What you need is footwear that lets you stay on the wall long enough to practise. A neutral shoe you can wear for two hours will improve your climbing far faster than an aggressive shoe you take off between every route.

Two other things matter more than most beginners realise. Stiffness supports your feet while the small stabilising muscles are still weak — soft shoes demand foot strength you have not built yet. And a flat, roomy toe box is what makes a shoe wearable, since the toes stay more or less straight rather than being crushed forward.

Sizing: The Advice That Ruins Most First Pairs

The single most damaging piece of received wisdom in climbing is that shoes should be agonisingly tight and will "stretch to fit". It is wrong often enough to be worth dismantling.

Shoes should be snug — no dead air, no heel lift, toes touching the end and gently curled rather than jammed. They should feel like a firm handshake, not a vice. REI's own coverage of the question, in a piece on why not to wear climbing shoes too tight, quotes instructors making the point directly: a shoe that fits properly does not stretch much, because nothing is forcing it to.

Stretch depends on material, and this is where the myth comes from. Unlined leather can stretch up to a full size, so a slightly tight fit is reasonable. Lined leather stretches perhaps half a size. Synthetic shoes barely stretch at all — what feels wrong in the shop will still feel wrong in a year. Most modern beginner shoes are synthetic or lined, so buy something you can actually wear.

Practical sizing notes: try shoes on in the afternoon, when feet are slightly larger. Wear them barefoot or in the thinnest possible sock, which is how you will climb. Stand up and put weight through your toes — a shoe that feels fine sitting down can be unbearable weighted. Walk a few steps. And ignore street size entirely; climbing shoe sizing varies wildly between brands, so someone who takes a 42 in trainers might be a 40 in one climbing brand and a 42.5 in another.

Buy in person for a first pair if you possibly can. Most gyms have a shop, and being able to try six pairs is worth more than any online review, including this one.

Seven of the Best Climbing Shoes for Beginners

All neutral or lightly moderate, all widely available, all shoes that regularly get recommended to new climbers by people who fit shoes for a living. Described from specifications and long-standing reputation rather than a controlled test on our part.

1. La Sportiva Tarantulace — the default recommendation

Flat profile, hard-wearing rubber, and a lace closure that lets you tune the fit across the whole foot, which matters if your feet are an awkward shape. Comfortable enough for long gym sessions and cheap enough that scuffing it does not sting. If you want one recommendation and no further thought, this is it.

2. Black Diamond Momentum — best for hot gyms

A knit upper that actually breathes, which is unusual in a category defined by sweaty rubber. Flat, comfortable, velcro closure for quick on and off between routes. The knit moulds to the foot over time. Slightly less precise on very small edges than the Tarantulace, which is a trade most beginners will not notice.

3. Scarpa Origin — best for wider feet

Scarpa's last runs broader than La Sportiva's, and if you have tried other shoes and found the forefoot pinching, this is the one to try. Two velcro straps, flat profile, generously padded. Very comfortable, at the cost of a little sensitivity.

4. Evolv Defy / Elektra — best all-rounder for gym climbing

The Defy and its Elektra counterpart are staples of gym rental walls and personal kit alike. Synthetic upper that barely stretches, so what you buy is what you keep. Slightly stiffer than the Momentum, which helps on vertical walls with small footholds.

5. La Sportiva Finale — best for long outdoor days

Built for multi-pitch and trad climbing where you are in the shoes for hours. Leather upper that moulds to the foot, stiff sole, lace closure. If your climbing is heading outdoors rather than staying in the gym, this is the more useful buy.

6. Butora Endeavor — best for unusual foot shapes

Sold in explicitly narrow and wide versions rather than one compromise last, which solves a real problem. Comfortable, forgiving, and a good option for anyone who has struggled to find a shoe that fits at all.

7. Tenaya Tanta — most comfortable of the group

Tenaya has a reputation for comfort, and the Tanta is the beginner-friendly model. Soft, flat, and pleasant to wear for extended periods. Less durable than the Tarantulace, so expect to resole or replace sooner if you climb often.

Closure Types, and Why It Is Not Just Preference

Every shoe on this list uses one of three closures, and each suits a different kind of climbing.

Laces give the most adjustment. You can slacken the forefoot and tighten the ankle, or vice versa, which matters enormously if your feet are an awkward shape or if one foot is bigger than the other — as most people's are. Laces also let you loosen the shoe as your feet swell over a long day. The downside is time: you will not be taking them off between boulder problems. Best for outdoor climbing, multi-pitch, and anyone with hard-to-fit feet.

Velcro straps are the gym default for the obvious reason. On and off in seconds, which encourages you to actually take them off between climbs — good for your feet and good for the shoes. You give up fine adjustment; the straps tighten the midfoot and that is roughly it. Best for bouldering and gym sessions.

Slippers have no closure at all, just an elasticated opening. They are the most sensitive and the least supportive, which makes them a poor first shoe: they demand foot strength beginners have not built. Worth knowing about, worth avoiding for now.

For a first pair, velcro if you climb mainly indoors, laces if you expect to be outdoors or have fitting difficulties.

Foot Shape Matters More Than Brand Loyalty

The reason shoe recommendations vary so wildly between climbers is that brands build around different foot shapes, and there is no universally best last — only the one matching your foot.

Toe shape. If your big toe is clearly longest, most shoes will suit you, since that is what the standard asymmetric last assumes. If your second toe is longer, you may find the toe box pinches painfully and should look at rounder-toed models. If your first three toes are roughly level, you want a broad, square toe box, and narrow performance shoes will be miserable.

Volume. This is the dimension nobody thinks about — the overall three-dimensional space inside the shoe, distinct from length and width. A low-volume foot swims in a high-volume shoe even at the right length, giving heel lift and dead space over the instep. Many brands offer low-volume versions, historically labelled as women's models though the sizing has nothing to do with gender.

Rough brand tendencies: La Sportiva runs narrow with a pronounced asymmetric toe; Scarpa runs broader through the forefoot; Evolv sits somewhere in the middle; Butora sells explicit wide and narrow versions; Tenaya tends towards comfort and moderate volume.

The practical consequence is that a shoe your climbing partner swears by can be unwearable for you, and that is about anatomy rather than either of you being wrong. Try several brands rather than several models from one brand — you will learn more about your own foot in twenty minutes of trying shoes than in a month of reading.

What to Spend, and What Else You Need

A decent beginner shoe sits in the middle of the market — well below flagship performance models and well above the unbranded shoes that delaminate in a month. Paying more at this stage buys performance you cannot use yet.

One caveat on price at the bottom end. Very cheap unbranded shoes tend to use soft, fast-wearing rubber and thin, unsupportive midsoles, which is the worst combination for a beginner: you get no edging support while the sole disappears within a couple of months. The saving is real but short-lived, and a worn-through sole teaches bad footwork because you cannot trust the shoe to hold.

Buy new rather than used for a first pair. Second-hand shoes have moulded to somebody else's foot and worn unevenly, which teaches you nothing useful about your own fit. The exception is a barely-worn pair from someone who sized wrong, which is common enough to be worth watching for.

Beyond shoes, a first kit is short: a chalk bag and chalk, and comfortable clothes you can move in. Everything else — harness, belay device, helmet — you rent or borrow until you know you are sticking with it. Our rock climbing gear checklist for beginners sets out what to buy and in what order, and our chalk bag guide covers the one other purchase worth making early.

Breaking Them In and Making Them Last

New shoes are uncomfortable for the first few sessions. That is normal. Agony is not.

Wear them for twenty or thirty minutes at a time to start, taking them off between climbs. Leather softens and moulds within a handful of sessions; synthetics mostly stay as they are. If they still hurt sharply after three or four sessions, they are too small — that is information, not a test of character.

Skip the internet remedies. Hot water, hairdryers and showering in your shoes degrade the adhesives holding the rubber to the upper, and will shorten the life of the shoe considerably more than they improve the fit.

Making them last: take them off between climbs, both for your feet and because walking around in rubber soles wears them out faster than climbing does. Never walk outside in them — grit destroys the sole. Air them after every session rather than sealing them in a bag, which is where the smell comes from. Store them out of direct sun and away from radiators; heat kills rubber and adhesive.

When the rubber thins at the big toe but the upper is still sound, resole rather than replace. It costs a fraction of a new pair and preserves the fit you have broken in. Get it done before you wear through into the rand — past that point the repair is much more involved and more expensive.

When to Upgrade

Not on a schedule, and not because you have been climbing a year. Upgrade when a specific limitation shows up.

The honest signals: you are climbing steep overhanging terrain where you need the toe to hook and pull rather than just stand; you can feel your shoe rolling off small holds your technique should be able to use; or you are climbing several times a week and the extra precision would genuinely translate into grades.

The bad signals: someone at the gym said your shoes were beginner shoes; you plateaued and want to buy your way through it; the shoes look unfashionable. Plateaus are almost always technique, fingers or fear, and none of those has a footwear solution.

Most climbers keep their comfortable neutral pair even after buying something aggressive, because warm-ups, long sessions and easy outdoor routes are all more pleasant in them. A first pair is rarely wasted money.

Frequently Asked Questions

How tight should beginner climbing shoes be?

Snug with no dead space, toes touching the end and slightly curled, no heel lift when you stand — but not painful. You should be able to keep them on for a twenty to thirty minute stretch without needing to rip them off. The old advice about sizing down two full sizes came from an era of unlined leather shoes that stretched enormously; most modern beginner shoes are synthetic or lined and will not stretch anywhere near that much.

Should beginners buy aggressive downturned shoes?

No. Downturned shoes concentrate force on the big toe for steep terrain, and in your first year you will be on vertical or slabby walls where they offer no advantage and considerable discomfort. They also encourage you to muscle through moves rather than learning to place your feet precisely, which is exactly the habit a beginner should avoid. Buy a flat shoe, learn footwork properly, and reassess in a year.

How long do climbing shoes last?

For someone climbing once or twice a week, roughly six months to a year before the toe rubber needs attention. Gym climbing wears shoes faster than most people expect, because textured plastic holds are abrasive. Resoling extends life substantially and costs far less than replacing.

Can I wear socks with climbing shoes?

You can, and some people do for hygiene in rental shoes or warmth on cold multi-pitch days, but it reduces sensitivity and the fit is calculated for a bare foot. If you want socks, size accordingly and use the thinnest you can find.

Are expensive climbing shoes better for beginners?

No — often the opposite. Expensive shoes are usually aggressive, soft performance models built for climbers with strong feet and precise technique. A mid-priced neutral shoe will serve a beginner better in every way that matters, and will hurt less while doing it.

Final Thoughts on the Best Climbing Shoes for Beginners

The best climbing shoes for beginners are flat, moderately stiff, comfortable enough to keep on between climbs, and cheap enough that you are not precious about scuffing them. That description fits every shoe on this list, and the differences between them come down mostly to foot shape — which is exactly why trying them on beats reading about them.

If you take one thing from this guide, make it the sizing point. Snug, not agonising. More people quit climbing over shoes that hurt than over anything that happens on the wall, and a first pair you actually enjoy wearing will do more for your progress than any amount of rubber technology.

posts.title: Best Climbing Harness for Beginners: How to Choose
posts.excerpt: The best climbing harness for beginners comes down to fit, not specs. Every certified harness is safe — here is what actually differs, and how to choose.
posts.content:
Choosing the best climbing harness for beginners is one of the easier gear decisions in climbing, and the internet makes it feel much harder than it is. Every certified harness on the market will hold a fall. What separates them is comfort, adjustability and how well they suit the kind of climbing you are actually going to do.

So this guide skips the spec-sheet arms race and works through the things that will genuinely affect your first year: fit, leg loop style, gear loops, and the small number of features worth paying for. That is a fair test for the best climbing harness for beginners.

Safety Is the Baseline, Not the Differentiator

First, the thing that removes most of the anxiety. It is one of the things that defines the best climbing harness for beginners.

Climbing harnesses sold in Europe are certified to EN 12277, and many carry UIAA certification alongside it. The standard defines four types — Type A full body, Type B small body, Type C sit harness and Type D chest harness — and requires tensile testing on every attachment point, with forces held for minutes at levels far beyond anything a climbing fall generates. Keep it in mind when shortlisting the best climbing harness for beginners.

A Type C sit harness is what nearly every recreational climber wears. The practical consequence is that a budget certified harness is not less safe than a premium one. You are paying for comfort, weight and features, not for strength. This is where the best climbing harness for beginners differs from a specialist one.

What does matter for safety is inspection and retirement. Check the tie-in points and belay loop for fuzziness or cuts before each session, and replace the harness when the wear indicators show through or after roughly seven to ten years regardless of use, since the webbing degrades with age. Our guide on when to retire climbing gear covers the signs. Judge the best climbing harness for beginners on this rather than the spec sheet.

Fit: The Only Thing That Really Matters

Fit is the whole decision, and it is the thing you cannot judge from a review. Most advice on the best climbing harness for beginners skips it.

The waistbelt sits above your hip bones, not on them and not around your waist like a belt. It should be snug enough that you cannot pull it down over your hips, with roughly a flat hand's width of space to breathe. It applies to the best climbing harness for beginners generally.

The buckle should end up near the middle of its adjustment range once tightened. At either extreme, the harness is the wrong size — and at the very end of the webbing you may not have enough tail left to be safe on older buckle designs. That is a fair test for the best climbing harness for beginners.

Leg loops should take two fingers underneath comfortably. Too tight restricts circulation on a long hang; too loose lets you slide. It is one of the things that defines the best climbing harness for beginners.

Hang in it before you buy. Most shops have a rig for this. Five minutes hanging tells you more than any amount of reading, because pressure points that are invisible standing up become obvious in thirty seconds of suspension. Keep it in mind when shortlisting the best climbing harness for beginners.

Body shape matters more than size charts admit. Harnesses cut for a narrower waist-to-hip ratio suit many women better regardless of what the label says, and there is no reason to restrict yourself to a section of the shop. This is where the best climbing harness for beginners differs from a specialist one.

Adjustable or Fixed Leg Loops?

The most common beginner question, and the answer is genuinely situational. Judge the best climbing harness for beginners on this rather than the spec sheet.

Adjustable leg loops let you accommodate winter layers, a big variation in clothing, or a body that is still changing shape. They also make it easier to share a harness within a family or a club. The cost is a little more weight and a bit more faff. Most advice on the best climbing harness for beginners skips it.

Fixed leg loops are lighter, simpler, and often more comfortable because there is no buckle sitting against your thigh. Excellent for indoor climbing and summer sport routes, less flexible if you climb through the winter in trousers. It applies to the best climbing harness for beginners generally.

For most people looking for the best climbing harness for beginners, adjustable wins on flexibility in the first year — you do not yet know what climbing you will end up doing, and adjustability buys you time to find out.

Gear Loops: How Many You Actually Need

Gear loops are the plastic or webbing loops around the waistbelt, and they are where harnesses differentiate themselves by discipline. That is a fair test for the best climbing harness for beginners.

Two loops is the gym and bouldering-plus-toprope minimum. Enough for a belay device, a couple of screwgates and a chalk bag. It is one of the things that defines the best climbing harness for beginners.

Four loops is the sport-climbing standard and the sensible default. Room for a full rack of quickdraws, plus your belay kit. Keep it in mind when shortlisting the best climbing harness for beginners.

Five or more, plus haul loops and ice clipper slots, is trad and alpine territory. Genuinely useful there, and dead weight if you are climbing indoors. This is where the best climbing harness for beginners differs from a specialist one.

Loop stiffness matters more than people expect. Rigid front loops make it much easier to clip a quickdraw one-handed while pumped; softer rear loops sit more comfortably against your back when you are wearing a pack. Judge the best climbing harness for beginners on this rather than the spec sheet.

Padding, Weight and Construction

Where the money goes. Most advice on the best climbing harness for beginners skips it.

Padding. More is more comfortable when hanging and working routes, and warmer and bulkier when moving. Wide, thin, breathable waistbelts have largely replaced thick foam in modern designs and generally distribute load better than raw thickness does. It applies to the best climbing harness for beginners generally.

Construction method. Traditional harnesses sew webbing onto foam; newer designs weave load-bearing fibres in a way that spreads force across the whole belt. The latter tends to be lighter and more comfortable, and costs more. That is a fair test for the best climbing harness for beginners.

Weight. Largely irrelevant indoors and at the crag. It starts to matter on long alpine days, which is not where you are starting. It is one of the things that defines the best climbing harness for beginners.

Belay loop. Check it is comfortably sized for a screwgate plus a belay device. Some minimalist harnesses have loops that get crowded. Keep it in mind when shortlisting the best climbing harness for beginners.

A reasonable rule when comparing the best climbing harness for beginners options: pick comfort over weight every time at this stage. You will spend more time hanging and learning than moving fast.

Features Worth Having and Ones You Can Ignore

Worth having: a drop-seat or rear elastic release if you will ever be in a harness for a full day; a haul loop, which is useful for a shoe bag or a second rope even indoors; and clearly marked tie-in points with visible wear indicators. This is where the best climbing harness for beginners differs from a specialist one.

Nice but not essential: ice clipper slots, an integrated gear rack, colour-coded buckles. Judge the best climbing harness for beginners on this rather than the spec sheet.

Genuinely ignorable at this stage: ultralight fabrics, minimalist alpine cuts with no padding, and anything marketed on gram counts. These are optimisations for problems you do not have. Most advice on the best climbing harness for beginners skips it.

One real caution: do not buy a used harness unless you know its full history. Webbing degrades with UV exposure, chemical contact and age, and none of that is visible. This is the one piece of climbing kit where secondhand is a false economy. Our overview of rock climbing gear for beginners covers what else is worth buying new. It applies to the best climbing harness for beginners generally.

Matching the Harness to Your Climbing

The best climbing harness for beginners depends on where you will actually be, and most people know this better than they think.

Indoor gym and toproping. Comfort and simplicity. Two gear loops is plenty, padding is welcome because you will hang a lot while learning, and adjustability helps if you climb year-round in varying kit. That is a fair test for the best climbing harness for beginners.

Outdoor sport climbing. Four gear loops, decent padding for belaying long pitches, and rigid front loops for clipping draws. It is one of the things that defines the best climbing harness for beginners.

Trad and multi-pitch. More loops, a haul loop, and a waistbelt that stays comfortable under a pack for hours. Keep it in mind when shortlisting the best climbing harness for beginners.

Alpine and ice. Adjustable legs for layering, ice clipper slots, and lighter construction. Not a first harness. This is where the best climbing harness for beginners differs from a specialist one.

Most beginners are in the first two categories, which is why a mid-range four-loop adjustable harness is the safest single recommendation across the whole category. Judge the best climbing harness for beginners on this rather than the spec sheet.

Putting It On Correctly

Worth stating because a well-chosen harness worn wrong is not safe. Most advice on the best climbing harness for beginners skips it.

Step in with both leg loops untwisted and the gear loops facing outward, pull the waistbelt above your hip bones, and tighten it before the legs. Check the belt is centred so the tie-in points sit at your front rather than off to one side. That is a fair test for the best climbing harness for beginners.

Then check the buckles. Modern auto-locking buckles need no doubling back, but older designs do, and a buckle that has not been doubled back can slip under load. If in doubt, ask — every instructor and every experienced climber at the wall will happily check it for you, and nobody will think less of you for asking. That is a fair test for the best climbing harness for beginners.

Finally, a partner check before every climb: harness buckled and doubled back where required, knot tied through both tie-in points, belay device correctly loaded and the screwgate locked. It is one of the things that defines the best climbing harness for beginners.

Budget: What You Get at Each Level

Honest framing rather than specific prices, which move constantly.

Entry level. Certified, safe, functional. Usually two to four gear loops, simpler padding, a bit heavier. Completely adequate for a first year of gym and sport climbing, and the sensible choice if you are not yet sure climbing will stick. Keep it in mind when shortlisting the best climbing harness for beginners.

Mid range. Better padding distribution, more thoughtful gear loop stiffness, adjustable legs, lighter materials. This is where most people end up, and where the comfort gain per pound spent is largest.

High end. Woven construction, very light, discipline-specific features. Worth it when you know your discipline; wasted money before then. This is where the best climbing harness for beginners differs from a specialist one.

The trap to avoid is buying a specialised harness before you know your discipline. A light alpine harness bought for gym climbing is uncomfortable in exactly the situation you will use it in.

Caring for It So It Lasts

A harness is cheap relative to the rest of your kit and it lasts years if you treat it sensibly. Judge the best climbing harness for beginners on this rather than the spec sheet.

Keep it out of the sun. UV is the main enemy of nylon webbing and it does its damage invisibly. A harness left hanging in a sunny window for a season has lost strength you cannot see. Store it in a bag or a dark cupboard.

Keep chemicals away from it. Battery acid is the classic hazard, which is why a harness should never travel loose in a car boot next to tools or a leisure battery. Petrol, solvents and bleach all attack nylon. Any known chemical contact means retirement, no matter how the webbing looks. Most advice on the best climbing harness for beginners skips it.

Wash it occasionally. Lukewarm water, mild non-detergent soap, rinse thoroughly, and dry away from direct heat and sunlight. Chalk and grit ground into the webbing act as an abrasive over time.

Do not store it damp. Wet webbing in a sealed bag encourages mildew, and while mildew is not itself a strength issue it is a sign the harness has been stored badly. It applies to the best climbing harness for beginners generally.

Log the purchase date. A marker pen on the label, or a note in your phone. The retirement clock runs from manufacture rather than from first use, and in ten years you will not remember. It is one of the things that defines the best climbing harness for beginners.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best climbing harness for beginners on a budget?

An entry-level certified sit harness with four gear loops and adjustable leg loops covers gym, toprope and sport climbing without compromise on safety. Every harness sold to EN 12277 has passed the same tensile testing, so a cheaper harness is not weaker — it is heavier, less refined in its padding and less specialised. Spend the difference on shoes, where the performance gap between budget and mid-range is far more noticeable. That is a fair test for the best climbing harness for beginners.

How do I know if a climbing harness fits properly?

The waistbelt sits above your hip bones and cannot be pulled down over them, with about a hand's width of breathing room. The buckle should sit near the middle of its adjustment range when tightened, not at either extreme. Two fingers should slide comfortably under the leg loops. Then hang in it for five minutes in the shop — pressure points that are invisible standing up become obvious quickly under suspension. That is a fair test for the best climbing harness for beginners.

Should I buy adjustable or fixed leg loops?

Adjustable, for a first harness. You do not yet know whether you will be climbing indoors in shorts or outdoors in winter trousers, and adjustable loops cover both. Fixed loops are lighter and slightly more comfortable, and they are a good second harness once your climbing has settled into a pattern. The weight difference is irrelevant at the level where this question comes up.

How long does a climbing harness last?

Manufacturers generally give seven to ten years from date of manufacture even if unused, because webbing degrades with age, and considerably less with heavy use. Retire it immediately if you can see coloured wear indicator threads at the tie-in points or belay loop, if there is fuzzing or a cut anywhere on a load-bearing element, or if it has contacted chemicals. Inspect before every session — it takes ten seconds. That is a fair test for the best climbing harness for beginners.

Can I use a bouldering harness for rope climbing?

There is no such thing as a bouldering harness — bouldering does not use one. What people usually mean is a very minimal sit harness, and provided it is certified to EN 12277 as a Type C it is safe for rope climbing. It will simply be uncomfortable if you hang in it, which is exactly what you do while learning. Comfort is the reason to choose otherwise, not safety.

Final Thoughts

The best climbing harness for beginners is a certified Type C sit harness that fits you properly, has four gear loops and adjustable legs, and feels comfortable when you hang in it for five minutes in the shop. That is the whole specification.

Safety is not the variable — every certified harness clears the same bar by an enormous margin. Comfort and fit are the variables, and neither can be judged from a spec sheet. Go and hang in a few, buy the one that disappears when you are wearing it, and put the money you saved into a decent pair of climbing shoes instead.
